Cold fusion. When it was announced for the first time, I really thought we had found a limitless source of clean, cheap energy that would carry us into the 21st century. I still think cold fusion is real, but it is obviously a lot more difficult to demonstrate and sustain than was initially believed, and it is not going to be the answer to all our energy woes.

Nuclear reactions are extremely energetic - much more energetic than even the most powerful chemical reactions. This is why you can use a significantly smaller amount of fuel to produce the same amount of energy as a chemical reaction.

This is because the chemical bonds that hold together molecules which get broken in chemical reactions only involve the electric force whereas the force that binds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus is much much stronger. The strength of the force correlates with the energy gained by forming or breaking those bonds. Consider by analogy the idea of dropping a person from 50 ft off the surface of the moon vs on the earth. In the earth's case that would almost certainly be fatal. The moon, not so much, provided the suit didn't break or tear.

At the molecular/atomic scale when these bonds are broken or formed, if it is a reaction that releases energy then there will be photons that are emitted carrying some of that energy. In the case of chemical reactions these photons aren't very energetic and they often fall into the visible spectrum. For example, a typical fire. In the case of nuclear reactions, if you're fusing elements lighter than iron or fission with elements heavier than iron then it will produce much more energetic radiation - photons with much higher frequency. This radiation can Pierce your flesh and slam into your dna molecules breaking those bonds. The genetic mutations resulting can often lead to cancers or other health problems. This effect will occur regardless of the temperature at which the reaction takes place. Period. Non negotiable.

But the real problem is that the electric force which repels like charges is pretty strong and the closer two particles with the same charge get to each other the stronger their repulsive effect. Thus the nucleii to be bonded must be travelling very rapidly at each other in order for their momentum to overpower the repulsive effect long enough to get entrapped by the stronger "strong" force that only acts over shorter distances. At all but the highest temperatures, we are unlikely to find any particles that have enough energy to break through this 'barrier'. Luckily we can get some help by the "quantum tunneling" effect but the chances of that occurring are quite small and the faster the particles are travelling the higher the chance. Also, the higher the pressure the more likely we will get one of these tunneling events. Even then they're somewhat rare. Even at the core of the sun, these events are unlikely enough that the sun will continue for billions of years before burning through all its fuel. If this weren't the case, the sun would go kaboom all at once.

Cold fusion is the claim that somehow, we can get this tunnelling effect to occur with mind boggling frequency even at low temperatures and pressures. I've studied a moderate amount of quantum mechanics and I know of no possible mechanism for this to happen, nor have I heard any explanation of how it might happen.
